title: The Gates That Were Never Delivered: from the Petite École to the Grave at Meudon
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Mouffetard Quarter and the Petite École

stops.name: Rue de l'Arbalète, the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: A son is born on the twelfth of November at number 3, rue de l'Arbalete, five floors up a narrow street in the Mouffetard quarter below the Pantheon. His father is a clerk in the prefecture of police, his mother a seamstress; the household is poor and devout, and holds no trade in it but the pen and the needle. Two days later, in another quarter of the same city, Claude Monet is born. The registers take down Francois Auguste Rene Rodin. He is called Auguste. He is nearsighted from childhood and holds whatever he is working on up close under his eyes to see it at all.
suggested_refs: The house at 3 rue de l'Arbalète, Mouffetard quarter, Paris

stops.name: Beauvais, the pension of his uncle
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Grunfeld gives 1851-1853; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: His parents send him to board at a pension in Beauvais kept by his uncle Jean-Hyppolite Rodin. He is judged a poor student: he cannot see the board, he cannot spell, and he draws through every lesson. Over the roofs of the school stands the choir of Saint-Pierre, the tallest Gothic vault ever raised and never finished, its nave never built at all. Nobody records whether the boy climbs it. He goes home to Paris after three years, still unable to spell, and is entered the following year at a school where the whole day is drawing.
suggested_refs: The unfinished choir of Beauvais cathedral, standing over the school
sources: Frédéric V. Grunfeld, 'Rodin: A Biography' (1987), relayed; primary text not consulted

stops.name: The Petite École, rue de l'École-de-Médecine
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: At fourteen he enters the Ecole speciale de dessin et de mathematiques on the Left Bank, the school the city calls the Petite Ecole. Its masters were trained in the eighteenth-century decorative tradition and let him work from memory and from the living model instead of copying plaster casts, a habit the great academy across the river has abolished. He fills notebooks in the Louvre and the Cabinet des estampes, and studies under Horace Lecoq de Boisbaudran. These three years are the only formal training he will ever receive.
stops.quote: The artist, on the contrary, sees; that is to say, that his eye, grafted on his heart, reads deeply into the bosom of Nature.
stops.quote_source: Auguste Rodin, 'Art: Conversations with Paul Gsell', trans. Mrs. Romilly Fedden (1912), Chapter I
suggested_refs: The Petite École, rue de l'École-de-Médecine, and Lecoq de Boisbaudran's memory-drawing method

stops.name: École des Beaux-Arts, three refusals
stops.date_confidence: attested: three refusals across 1857-1859; exact dates not recorded, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: He carries a modelled clay figure to the Ecole des Beaux-Arts and is refused. He returns and is refused again, and a third time. The examiners find the work rough, the handling of light on flesh too free; the school that trains every sculptor of consequence in France will not have him. He is seventeen at the first refusal and nineteen at the last. For the next twenty years he works as an ornamenter, a craftsman for hire, cutting other men's designs under other men's signatures. He does not show anything at a Salon under his own name until he is thirty-six.
suggested_refs: The entrance at 14 rue Bonaparte, École nationale supérieure des Beaux-Arts
sources: coordinates corrected against the school's rue Bonaparte entrance

stops.name: Congregation of the Blessed Sacrament, the year in the habit
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: His sister Maria dies of peritonitis. Rodin, twenty-two and undone, gives up art and enters the Congregation of the Blessed Sacrament as a laybrother, in a habit and a routine of prayer. The founder of the order, Father Pierre-Julien Eymard, watches him for a few months and tells him plainly that his vocation is not the cloister. Rodin leaves within the year and models the head of the priest who sent him back to the clay: the first work of his hand that can be dated. He goes back to Paris and to piecework in plaster, and never takes vows in any order again.
suggested_refs: The bust of Father Pierre-Julien Eymard, 1863, Rodin's first datable work
sources: Musée Rodin, official biography (for Eymard's counsel, reported as the order's tradition)

stops.name: The atelier of Carrier-Belleuse, and Rose Beuret
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: He enters the studio of Albert-Ernest Carrier-Belleuse, who supplies busts, vases, candelabra and architectural ornament to the whole trade of the Second Empire. Rodin works fast and anonymously; his hand disappears into objects sold under his employer's name for the next fourteen years. The same year he meets Rose Beuret, a seamstress from the Haute-Marne, who begins to model for him and does not stop. Their son Auguste-Eugene is born in 1866. Rose stays with him through every studio and every other woman, and the two of them die in the same year, 1917.
stops.quote: The artist must have the patience of water that eats away the rock drop by drop.
stops.quote_source: Judith Cladel, 'Rodin: The Man and His Art' (English trans., 1917), p. 7
suggested_refs: Carrier-Belleuse's Second Empire ornament trade, in which Rodin's early work is anonymous

stops.name: Théâtre des Gobelins, unsigned stone
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: He carves decorative bas-reliefs for the facade of the new theatre on the avenue des Gobelins, in the tanners' quarter of the thirteenth arrondissement. It is ordinary contract stone of the kind that has paid his rent all decade, and nothing on it carries his name. He is twenty-nine. Paris is by now full of buildings with his work on them and no one in Paris knows it. He will remain unknown for another eight years, and the thing that finally ends the anonymity is a charge of fraud.
stops.quote: It is necessary to have consummate technique in order to hide what one knows.
stops.quote_source: Auguste Rodin, 'Art: Conversations with Paul Gsell', trans. Mrs. Romilly Fedden (1912)
suggested_refs: The façade reliefs of the Théâtre des Gobelins, avenue des Gobelins, Paris

segments.name: The Siege, Brussels, and the Italian Journey

stops.name: The eastern ramparts, the National Guard
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1870; September stands for the opening of the siege, the day of enrolment is not recorded
stops.campa: France is at war with Prussia and Rodin is mobilised into the National Guard on the eastern ramparts, a corporal in a city preparing to be surrounded. He is thirty and so shortsighted that he cannot aim; he is discharged before the siege is far advanced. The siege empties Paris of patrons, of commissions and of bread. Within months there is no ornamental work left in the capital for a man who lives by ornamental work, and he follows Carrier-Belleuse north into Belgium, where the building is still going on.
suggested_refs: The 1870 siege of Paris and the National Guard levies of the eastern quarters
sources: corrected: the pool filed the Guard service and the Brussels move both under 1871

stops.name: Bourse de Bruxelles, six years as his own master
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the month is a reconstruction
stops.campa: He arrives in Brussels to carve the decorative sculpture of the new stock exchange, allegorical groups on a building raised to money. When Carrier-Belleuse goes back to Paris, Rodin stays, forming a partnership with the Belgian sculptor Antoine van Rasbourgh, under whose name the joint work is signed in Belgium and under Rodin's in France. Six years pass here, the longest stretch he will ever spend outside Paris. It is the first time he works as his own master, and out of a craftsman's wage he saves the fare to Italy.
suggested_refs: The caryatids and allegorical groups of the Brussels Bourse
The Rodin and van Rasbourgh partnership, 1871-1877
sources: Frédéric V. Grunfeld, 'Rodin: A Biography' (1987), for the van Rasbourgh partnership

stops.name: Piazza dei Miracoli, Pisa
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the two-month journey falls in 1875, the internal dates are not recorded
stops.campa: He crosses the Alps in spring on a strict budget and moves fast: Turin, Genoa, Pisa, Florence, Rome, Naples, Venice in roughly eight weeks. At Pisa he studies the Camposanto and the cathedral pulpits, looking less at any single monument than at how the men who cut them let light break across a carved surface. He is thirty-four, a master craftsman by trade and an unknown by reputation, travelling alone with a sketchbook to see in stone what he has copied all his life from casts and engravings.
suggested_refs: The Camposanto and the Pisano pulpits, Piazza dei Miracoli
sources: Frédéric V. Grunfeld, 'Rodin: A Biography' (1987), for the itinerary

stops.name: The Medici Chapel, Florence
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: within the 1875 journey, exact date not recorded
stops.campa: In the New Sacristy of San Lorenzo he stands before Michelangelo's dukes and their sprawling allegories of Day, Night, Dawn and Dusk, and afterwards says that Michelangelo freed him from the academy. He does not copy the manner. What he takes is the licence to leave a surface unresolved, to let the marks of the making stay on the figure where the academy would have polished them off. For the next forty years he sends out torsos still rough where the chisel stopped. He works over the drawings he made in this room for years afterwards.
stops.quote: In the drawing of Michael Angelo it is not his manner, not the audacious foreshortening nor the skilful anatomy that should be admired, but the desperate force of the Titan.
stops.quote_source: Auguste Rodin, 'Art: Conversations with Paul Gsell', trans. Mrs. Romilly Fedden (1912)
suggested_refs: Michelangelo's Medici tombs, New Sacristy of San Lorenzo, Florence

stops.name: Rome, the antique seen at last
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: within the 1875 journey, month not recorded
stops.campa: He reaches Rome and sees in the flesh the antique sculpture he has drawn from plaster since he was fourteen at the Petite Ecole. The city becomes a recurring address in a life otherwise fixed on Paris and its suburbs: he will return in 1911 to see his own Walking Man set up at the Palazzo Farnese, and again in 1915, at seventy-four and in the middle of a world war, to model a pope. Within weeks he goes back north to Brussels and begins the standing figure that will break him into public notice.
suggested_refs: The antique collections of Rome, known to Rodin until 1875 only through casts

segments.name: The Age of Bronze and the Accusation

stops.name: Fairmount Park, the Philadelphia Centennial
stops.date_confidence: attested for the exposition; 10 May stands for its opening, the date of Rodin's entry is not recorded
stops.campa: A cast of Rodin's work is shipped to the Centennial Exposition in Philadelphia, one entry among thousands at the first world's fair the United States holds. He does not go. The piece travels as freight, is unremarked, and is the first of his sculptures to cross an ocean without him. He never sees it again. For forty years afterwards the bronzes leave in crates, are unloaded and set on pedestals in cities he does not visit, and stand there under his name while he stays between the rue de l'Universite and Meudon.
suggested_refs: The 1876 Centennial Exposition, Fairmount Park, Philadelphia

stops.name: Cercle Artistique et Littéraire, Brussels: the accusation begins
stops.date_confidence: attested for January 1877; the day is not recorded, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: He exhibits a standing male nude modelled over eighteen months from a young Belgian soldier named Auguste Neyt. The figure is called The Vanquished, then The Age of Bronze. Its naturalism is so complete that a whisper starts here and travels with the sculpture: that no man could have modelled this, that Rodin has cast it from a living body, a surmoulage, a fraud. He is thirty-six and unknown. If the charge holds, everything he makes afterwards is taken to be a plaster shell pulled off somebody's back.
suggested_refs: The photographs of Auguste Neyt in the pose, kept by the Musée Rodin

stops.name: The Paris Salon, the surmoulage answered
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1877 Salon; the day is not recorded
stops.campa: He brings the figure to the Paris Salon and the whisper becomes a charge in print. He answers with photographs of Neyt standing in the pose, with measurements, with the testimony of anyone who watched him work; two years pass before the state accepts that the sculpture was made and not moulded. More people know his name after the charge than before it. He comes back from Belgium with Rose Beuret and settles on the Left Bank at thirty-seven, known at last, and known for this.
stops.quote: I obey Nature in everything, and I never pretend to command her. My only ambition is to be servilely faithful to her.
stops.quote_source: Auguste Rodin, 'Art: Conversations with Paul Gsell', trans. Mrs. Romilly Fedden (1912), Chapter I
suggested_refs: 'L'Âge d'airain', 1877, and the two-year defence against the charge of casting from life

stops.name: Dépôt des marbres, the Gates of Hell commissioned
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: The state buys the disputed bronze and Edmond Turquet, undersecretary of fine arts, commissions from him a monumental door for a museum of decorative arts. Rodin is given a studio at the Depot des marbres, a royal marble store on the rue de l'Universite. He takes his subject from Dante and begins The Gates of Hell: two hundred figures writhing on a portal for a museum that is never built. The door is unfinished at his death thirty-seven years later, and nearly every famous single figure of his maturity is lifted out of it.
stops.quote: Art is the most sublime mission of man, since it is the expression of thought seeking to understand the world and to make it understood.
stops.quote_source: Auguste Rodin, 'Art: Conversations with Paul Gsell', trans. Mrs. Romilly Fedden (1912), Preface
suggested_refs: 'La Porte de l'Enfer', begun 1880, worked on until 1917 and never delivered

stops.name: London, the first crossing
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: The painter Alphonse Legros brings him to London and introduces him to the poet and critic William Ernest Henley, who begins arguing for him in English print before the French press has settled its opinion. Rodin learns etching from Legros on the same visit. The English connection opens here and never closes. It brings him English buyers while Paris is still deciding about him, a doctorate at Oxford twenty-six years from now, and in the end a room of his sculpture given outright to a country not his own.
suggested_refs: W. E. Henley's championing of Rodin in the English press from 1881

stops.name: Dépôt des marbres, Camille Claudel
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; pin inherited byte-identical from camille_claudel.journey.json, which differs from this file's other Dépôt des marbres coordinate; the divergence is flagged, not resolved
stops.campa: An eighteen-year-old sculptor is taken into his circle while he supervises a course for young students. Camille Claudel becomes his praticienne, cutting marble for the Burghers of Calais; she models for the Gates of Hell; she makes work of her own that the critics keep mistaking for his. She is also his lover for the next decade, against Rose Beuret at Meudon, and the unravelling of it through the 1890s marks both of them permanently. He is forty-three. She works beside him for a decade and leaves to work alone, and the studios of Paris keep the two bodies of work confused for a century.
suggested_refs: Camille Claudel's hands and feet in the Gates of Hell; her marble cutting for the Burghers

stops.name: Jackson Park, the Columbian Exposition
stops.date_confidence: attested for the exposition; the day of Rodin's showing is not recorded
stops.campa: His sculpture crosses the Atlantic a second time without him, to the great white fair in Jackson Park. Some pieces are hung with curtains, judged too frank in their nudity for the fairground public, and shown only to those who ask for them. The quarrel that follows him in Paris has followed the plaster to Illinois: the objection is never to the subject, always to how little the surface conceals. He is fifty-three and expects it by now. American collectors start buying him regardless.
stops.quote: To any artist, worthy of the name, all in nature is beautiful, because his eyes, fearlessly accepting all exterior truth, read there, as in an open book, all the inner truth.
stops.quote_source: Auguste Rodin, 'Art: Conversations with Paul Gsell', trans. Mrs. Romilly Fedden (1912), Chapter II
suggested_refs: The curtained Rodin exhibits at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, Chicago

stops.name: Giverny, at Monet's table
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year by fr.wikipedia; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Claude Monet invites him to the house and garden at Giverny. The two men were born in Paris two days apart in November 1840, and five years before this they showed together at the Galerie Georges Petit, the exhibition where the Burghers of Calais were seen in public for the first time. Both men are being told by critics that their work is unfinished, one in paint and one in bronze, and neither of them accepts the charge. Rodin is difficult company at the table and is asked back anyway.
suggested_refs: The 1889 Monet-Rodin exhibition, Galerie Georges Petit, Paris
sources: Wikipedia (English), 'Claude Monet', for the two-day gap in their births

stops.name: Villa des Brillants, the house at Meudon
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of purchase; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: He buys a plain brick house on a hill southwest of Paris, above the Seine at Meudon, and moves Rose Beuret into it. The grounds fill with plaster: casts, fragments of antique columns bought off demolition sites, whole rooms of working models, and eventually the pavilion of his 1900 exhibition carted out from Paris and rebuilt on the lawn. He works there, stores his casts there and keeps house there, and in twenty-two years he is buried in the garden. The road below it is now called the avenue Auguste Rodin.
stops.quote_source: James Huneker, introduction to Judith Cladel, 'Rodin: The Man and His Art' (1917), reporting Rodin on the pace of Dutch life
suggested_refs: The Villa des Brillants and its plaster collections, 19 avenue Auguste Rodin, Meudon

stops.name: Calais, the burghers set down
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Eleven years after the commission the six burghers of 1347 are inaugurated at Calais, in front of the Parc Richelieu: barefoot men in rope halters carrying the keys of a starving town out to the English king, each one alone inside his own dread. Rodin wanted them at ground level without a pedestal, so that they would walk among the living. The town puts them on a high pedestal instead, against his wishes. He loses the argument in the city that commissioned them, and it is put right only much later, when the group is moved.
stops.quote: No one may benefit mankind with impunity.
stops.quote_source: James Huneker, introduction to Judith Cladel, 'Rodin: The Man and His Art' (1917), reporting Rodin
suggested_refs: 'Les Bourgeois de Calais', inaugurated 3 June 1895 before the Parc Richelieu, later moved before the Hôtel de Ville
sources: corrected: not the Hôtel de Ville in 1895, and the pedestal argument was lost

stops.name: Paris, the Balzac refused
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1898 Salon; the day is not recorded
stops.campa: Seven years after commissioning it, the Societe des Gens de Lettres sees the plaster Balzac: a head thrown back on a column of dressing gown, no hands, no body, a pillar of a man. The press calls it a snowman, a sack, a menhir. The Societe rejects it as unfinished. Rodin refuses a public subscription of thirty thousand francs raised to cast it, repays the commission, and carts the plaster out to his own garden at Meudon, where it stands among the fruit trees for the rest of his life.
stops.quote: In fact, in art, only that which has character is beautiful.
stops.quote_source: Auguste Rodin, 'Art: Conversations with Paul Gsell', trans. Mrs. Romilly Fedden (1912), Chapter II
suggested_refs: The rejected plaster 'Monument à Balzac', 1898, kept at Meudon

segments.name: Nineteen Hundred: the Pavilion and the Bronzes That Cross Without Him

stops.name: Parque Tres de Febrero, the Sarmiento unveiled
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the twenty-fifth of May a bronze Domingo Faustino Sarmiento is unveiled in the Parque Tres de Febrero at Palermo, brought to Argentina through the efforts of the museum director Eduardo Schiaffino. It stands on the ground of the Caseron de Rosas, the house of the dictator Sarmiento spent his life opposing, pulled down the year before on the anniversary of his fall. Rodin never crosses the ocean. Sarmiento died twelve years before the unveiling and never saw himself in bronze. The two men meet here, in a park, by proxy.
suggested_refs: The Monumento a Sarmiento, Avenidas Libertador and Sarmiento, Palermo, Buenos Aires
sources: Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Parque Tres de Febrero' and 'Eduardo Schiaffino'
the claim that it is his only work made expressly for Buenos Aires is brief-sourced and uncorroborated

stops.name: Pavillon de l'Alma, the retrospective he pays for himself
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; June stands for the opening alongside the Exposition Universelle
stops.campa: At sixty, at his own expense and outside the official grounds of the world's fair, he builds a pavilion by the Pont de l'Alma and fills it with a hundred and fifty of his own works. It is a gamble against the Salon and it works: the critics divide, the public does not, and he leaves the summer a phenomenon rather than a specialist controversy. Isadora Duncan comes through the pavilion and finds him; he draws her for years afterwards in the studio on the rue de l'Universite. Loie Fuller's theatre stands a few steps away.
suggested_refs: The Pavillon de l'Alma, later dismantled and rebuilt in the grounds at Meudon

stops.name: Paris, the sculptor as an industry
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the pattern has no single date, and December stands for the close of the exposition season
stops.campa: After the pavilion the portrait commissions arrive from every capital in Europe and from American money, and his studio takes in something near two hundred thousand francs a year. He employs praticiens to cut the marble, founders to pour the bronze and secretaries to answer in three languages; the work leaves the rue de l'Universite in crates. The man who spent twenty years cutting other men's designs anonymously now signs work that other hands have cut, and is asked, more than once, whether that is the same thing.
suggested_refs: The Rodin studio system of praticiens, founders and secretaries after 1900
sources: canonical Paris pin inherited from the atlas

stops.name: The Panthéon, the Thinker set before the dome
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of installation; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: The seated figure, enlarged four years earlier to somewhere between a hundred and eighty and a hundred and ninety centimetres and paid for by public subscription, is set down in front of the Pantheon as property of the city of Paris. It began as Dante at the lintel of the Gates, a poet looking down into his own damned; it was called The Poet before it was called The Thinker. The title has come loose from the man. The crowds who stop in front of it are not thinking of Florence, and about twenty-nine more of these are cast for public squares on four continents under the name it acquired by accident.
stops.quote: There is really neither beautiful style, nor beautiful drawing, nor beautiful color; there is but one sole beauty, that of the truth which is revealed.
stops.quote_source: Auguste Rodin, 'Art: Conversations with Paul Gsell', trans. Mrs. Romilly Fedden (1912), Chapter V
suggested_refs: The 1904 Salon enlargement of 'Le Penseur' and its subscription cast for the city of Paris
sources: height unresolved: 181 cm (en), 185 cm, or 189 cm (fr)

stops.name: Marseille, the Cambodian dancers
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; July stands for the royal ballet's appearance at the colonial exposition
stops.campa: The Royal Ballet of Cambodia performs at the colonial exposition and Rodin, sixty-five, follows the company for days with a block of paper, then follows it to Paris and back again. He works in pencil and wash at speed, catching the bent wrists and stepped knees of dancers whose bodies are trained to positions no European academy contains. He never returns to the subject after the company sails, and he never works this fast again: a few lines of graphite, a wash of colour, and nothing corrected afterwards.
stops.quote: Movement is the transition from one attitude to another.
stops.quote_source: Auguste Rodin, 'Art: Conversations with Paul Gsell', trans. Mrs. Romilly Fedden (1912), Chapter IV
suggested_refs: The 1906 Cambodian dancer drawings, Musée Rodin

stops.name: The Sheldonian Theatre, Oxford
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; June stands for the Encaenia, the exact day is not recorded
stops.campa: Oxford makes him a doctor of the university in the Sheldonian, in a red gown, before an audience of dons. He is sixty-six, the son of a police clerk, and was refused three times by the school of fine arts in his own city on the grounds that he could not model. The English relationships that carry him into this room opened twenty-six years earlier with Legros and Henley. Seven years from now he gives a room of sculpture to the British nation outright. He never gives anything to the school on the rue Bonaparte.
suggested_refs: Rodin's honorary doctorate, University of Oxford, 1907

stops.name: Plaza del Congreso, El Pensador
stops.date_confidence: attested for November 1907 by es.wikipedia, 'Plaza del Congreso'; the 1909 date in circulation has no source support and is rejected here; the day is not recorded
stops.campa: A bronze Thinker is inaugurated in the eastern half of the Plaza del Congreso, facing the Argentine parliament: one of two casts taken from the original mould and signed by Rodin's own hand. It is the second of his works standing in the open air of Buenos Aires, a few kilometres from Sarmiento in Palermo. Three years later Carlos Thays finishes redesigning the plaza around it for the centenary, laying his paths and lawns out to meet a bronze that is already in place and will not be moved for them.
suggested_refs: The Buenos Aires 'El Pensador', one of two casts from the original mould, signed by Rodin
sources: corrected: the pool credited this to es.wikipedia 'El pensador', which contains none of it

stops.name: Hôtel Biron, 77 rue de Varenne
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: He rents the ground floor of an eighteenth-century townhouse in the Faubourg Saint-Germain, let cheaply to anyone who will take it while the state decides whether to pull it down. Rainer Maria Rilke, who was his secretary at Meudon, found the place; Matisse and Cocteau have rooms upstairs. Rodin leaves Rose Beuret at Meudon and begins an affair with the American-born Duchesse de Choiseul, who manages his affairs and is later accused of milking them. The house he takes to work in becomes the museum of his name.
stops.quote_source: Rainer Maria Rilke, 'Auguste Rodin', trans. Jessie Lemont and Hans Trausil (New York: Sunwise Turn, 1919), reporting Rodin
suggested_refs: The Hôtel Biron, 77 rue de Varenne, before its rescue from demolition
sources: corrected: the address is 77, not 79, rue de Varenne

stops.name: Meudon, the letter to Loïe Fuller
stops.date_confidence: attested: the letter is dated from Meudon, 19 January 1908
stops.campa: He writes from Meudon to Loie Fuller, the American who dances inside hundreds of yards of lit silk, and calls her a woman of genius who has reawakened the spirit of antiquity. She prints the letter in her memoir, as anyone would. Eight years earlier her theatre stood a few steps from his pavilion at the world's fair, and the two of them have been circling one another since. He is sixty-seven, and in these years he draws dancers more often than he models anyone.
stops.quote_source: Rodin to Loïe Fuller, letter dated Meudon, 19 January 1908, printed in Fuller's memoir
suggested_refs: Loïe Fuller's memoir, printing Rodin's letter of 19 January 1908

stops.name: Palazzo Farnese, the Walking Man
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: A cast of the Walking Man is set up at the Palazzo Farnese, seat of the French embassy to Italy: a striding torso with no head and no arms, made by welding two abandoned studies together and declaring the join a work. It stands inside a High Renaissance palace whose cornice Michelangelo designed. Rodin first stood in front of Michelangelo's work thirty-six years earlier, in Florence, and came away certain that a fragment could be a finished thing. The proof of it is now parked under Michelangelo's roofline.
suggested_refs: 'L'Homme qui marche' at the Palazzo Farnese, Rome

stops.name: Théâtre du Châtelet, the Faune defended
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Vaslav Nijinsky dances the Afternoon of a Faun and ends it lying face down on a nymph's scarf. Le Figaro calls the piece filthy on its front page. Rodin, who has been drawing Nijinsky, answers in print that the dancer's body is sculpture in motion and that nobody should be scandalised; the same paper then turns on Rodin, an old man of seventy-one living rent-free in a state building and defending indecency. The attack nearly costs him the lease of the Hotel Biron.
suggested_refs: The Figaro campaign of May 1912 against 'L'Après-midi d'un Faune' and against Rodin

stops.name: Victoria Tower Gardens, the burghers at Westminster
stops.date_confidence: purchased 1911, positioned in the gardens 1914, unveiled 19 July 1915; the stop is dated to the placing, month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: A bronze cast of the Burghers of Calais, bought by the British government three years earlier, is placed in the gardens beside the Houses of Parliament and unveiled the following July, with the war a year old and the burghers' own town under German guns. The same year Rodin gives a group of his works to the British nation outright. Six medieval Frenchmen walking out to surrender their city stand within sight of Westminster, offering their keys to an English king in the year France and England go to war on the same side.

stops.name: The Vatican, the bust of Benedict XV
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: In the second year of the war he travels to Rome to model the head of Benedict XV. The pope, occupied with a continent killing itself and unpersuaded by the sculptor, grants him three or four short sittings and then stops. Rodin, seventy-four and failing, cannot finish. He leaves the clay as it stands and goes home to Meudon. It is among the last portraits of his life, and it is unfinished in the way half his work is unfinished, though this time not by his own decision.
suggested_refs: The unfinished bust of Pope Benedict XV, 1915, Musée Rodin

stops.name: Villa des Brillants, the marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the twenty-ninth of January, in the cold house at Meudon with the war in its fourth winter, Rodin marries Rose Beuret. She is seventy-three and has been in this house since 1895 and in his life since 1864, through Camille Claudel, through the Duchesse de Choiseul, through the fame and through the years of being introduced to nobody. He is seventy-six and can no longer manage his own affairs. A few friends attend. The marriage that took fifty-three years to arrive lasts less than three weeks.
suggested_refs: The marriage of Auguste Rodin and Rose Beuret, Meudon, 29 January 1917

stops.name: Villa des Brillants, the death of Rose Beuret
stops.date_confidence: sources conflict: fr.wikipedia ('Rose Beuret', 'Villa des Brillants') gives 14 February 1917, en.wikipedia gives 16 February; the conflict is flagged, not resolved
stops.campa: Rose Beuret dies at Meudon, sixteen or eighteen days married depending on which country's record is believed, of the bronchitis she took in a house nobody could heat that winter. She had modelled for him, kept his plasters damp, raised his son, and been left in the suburbs while he took rooms in town. In the accounts of his life she appears mostly as the woman Camille Claudel was set against. She had been in this house twenty-two years and had lived nowhere else since he bought it.
suggested_refs: Rose Beuret's grave in the grounds of the Villa des Brillants

stops.name: Villa des Brillants, the death of Rodin
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Nine months after Rose, in the same house, Rodin dies at seventy-seven of what the doctors call congestion of the lungs. The coal for the villa's stoves cannot be had; the state that owns his collection cannot heat the man who gave it. He has been confused and badly managed for two years. By the time he stops breathing his bronzes stand in Paris, London, Rome, Philadelphia, Chicago and Buenos Aires, and the door commissioned from him in 1880 is still lying in pieces in the studio.
suggested_refs: Rodin's death certificate and the wartime fuel shortage at Meudon
sources: corrected: congestion of the lungs, not influenza

stops.name: Meudon, the grave under the Thinker
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He is buried in the grounds of his own house beside Rose Beuret, a week after his death. Over the grave they set a monumental bronze Thinker, at his own wish: the figure lifted out of the Gates of Hell, first modelled as Dante looking down into his own poem, cast and recast for public squares on four continents, brought back to sit on top of the man who made it. Below the hill the plaster city of casts, fragments and bought columns stands exactly where he left it.
suggested_refs: The tomb of Rodin and Rose Beuret at the Villa des Brillants, with 'Le Penseur' as headstone

stops.name: Musée Rodin, the Hôtel Biron opened
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The house he rented in 1908, saved from demolition by the gift he made in 1916 of his works, his collections and his casting rights to the French state, opens to the public as the Musee Rodin. Two years of war lie between the founding law and the opening day. The garden takes the Gates of Hell and a Thinker; the rooms take the marbles, the drawings, the working plasters and the antiquities he bought with portrait money. The state that refused him a place at its school now administers his estate.
suggested_refs: The founding law of 1916 and the opening of the Musée Rodin, 4 August 1919

stops.name: Boulevard du Montparnasse, the Balzac cast at last
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Forty-one years after the Societe des Gens de Lettres called it grotesque, the Balzac is cast in bronze and set up at the crossing of the boulevard du Montparnasse and the boulevard Raspail, in the quarter where the writers who inherited Balzac drink. Rodin has been dead twenty-two years. In 1969 Kenneth Clark will call it the greatest piece of sculpture of the nineteenth century. It stands in the traffic on the spot it was refused for, at the size and in the material its author intended.
suggested_refs: The bronze 'Monument à Balzac', installed 2 July 1939, boulevard Raspail, Paris

stops.name: Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes, the contested Kiss
stops.date_confidence: one source dates the marble Kiss to a 1940s purchase, another calls it a gift from Rodin himself; the decade is used and the conflict left open, day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: A marble Kiss stands in the museum on the Avenida del Libertador. How it arrived is contested: one account has Rodin giving it himself, another has the museum buying it in the 1940s inside a larger purchase of European art. The house is said to hold nineteen Rodin sculptures and three drawings, which would make it one of the strongest holdings in the Americas, though the museum's own catalogue could not be opened to confirm the count. Neither version of the arrival is documented in anything reachable. The marble stands in the gallery under his name either way.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the city of bronzes
stops.date_confidence: no single date: the city's Rodin holdings accumulate across the twentieth century, and 1950 stands for the accumulation
stops.campa: Three Rodin addresses stand within a few kilometres of each other in a city he never visited: Sarmiento in the park at Palermo, the Thinker at the Congress, and the marbles and bronzes in the Bellas Artes. Argentine sculptors work in their shadow; Troiano Troiani's Archer of 1924, in the Plaza Moreno at La Plata, is read at once as Rodin's surface on another man's stance. The bronzes came by ship, were set on their pedestals by municipal crews, and were signed by a man who was in Meudon at the time.

stops.name: Avenue Matignon, the market for a Thinker
stops.date_confidence: attested for June 2022; the day of the sale is not recorded here
stops.campa: About twenty-nine monumental Thinkers stand in public places and museums from Copenhagen to Kyoto to Stanford, not all of them poured under Rodin's eye. French law allows twelve authorised casts of an edition after a sculptor's death; the Burghers of Calais stand in fourteen cities, and the arithmetic has never been reconciled in print. A forgery ring running fake Rodin bronzes was broken up in the 1990s and the dealer Guy Hain convicted in 2001. A Rudier cast of 1928 comes up for sale here, reported at up to fourteen million euros.
suggested_refs: The Christie's Paris sale of June 2022 and the Guy Hain forgery prosecutions
